chapter: The Raeburn band: people and touring
title: Bothwell the strange, handsome leader of the band
summary: Handy describes Bothwell's chicken-like Hodges imitation and the rift in the band.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: He was a very capable saxophone player. He was a strange guy.
In what way strange?
You never knew how he felt about things. For instance, we found it very hard, this instance that I told you about-- this was the Lincoln that that happened at, this

thing about everybody complimenting on how great he played and him telling us he purposely played badly just to show us how wrong we were. I wouldn't have expected that from him. That's kind of strange.
I don't know how you can do that. I wouldn't know how to play a bad chorus. That would take exquisite talent, I should think, to play something bad that was not--
Deliberately bad? Sure.
I don't know how you would do that. It may be a great testament to his skill.
Could be.
He always fancied himself as a Johnny Hodges sort of player. That's my understanding. I would think he would be pretty locked into style just because of that.
He did try to sound like Hodges, but he overdíd it, that's why he sounded like a chicken to me. I didn't pick that out as a kind way of being insulting. He really
Was he popular with the guys?

Yeah; he was a leader of the band, until these things began to happen, then it became Bothwell against the world. He started to keep to himself, stay away from the other guys and it was a musical thing that caused it.
He was extraordinarily handsome and charming; wasn't he?
A good looking guy. He was the ladies man.
Actively?
Actively.
Did that ever get in the way of the band, in the way of music?
No.
The guys kept their schedules, they didn't let anything interfere with their job or
their responsibilities, no matter what their inclinations were.
